title: The Frankfurt School and Hannah Arendt
subtitle: After catastrophe: thinking about reason, mass culture and the banality of evil
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain what critical theory is and how it differs from traditional theory.
By the end you will be able to describe Adorno and Horkheimer's critique of the culture industry and the dialectic of enlightenment.
By the end you will be able to explain Habermas's idea of the public sphere and why he thought it had decayed.
By the end you will be able to outline Arendt's analysis of totalitarianism and her concept of the banality of evil.
By the end you will be able to assess major criticisms of both the Frankfurt School and Arendt.
hook:
In April 1961, in a courtroom in Jerusalem, a balding man in a grey suit sat inside a glass booth, built to protect him. He was Adolf Eichmann, the SS officer who had organised the deportation of millions of Jews to the death camps. Everyone expected to see a monster. Hannah Arendt, a German-Jewish refugee philosopher reporting on the trial for *The New Yorker*, saw something she found more frightening: a dull, ambitious bureaucrat who spoke in clichés and seemed never to have really thought about what he was doing. She called it **the banality of evil**, and the phrase has haunted moral thought ever since.

Arendt was one of several German-Jewish thinkers forced into exile by Hitler who spent the rest of their lives asking how a modern, educated, scientific society could produce Auschwitz. Another group, known as the Frankfurt School, asked a related question: why had the Enlightenment's promise of reason and freedom led not to liberation but to new forms of domination? Today's lesson brings them together.

sections.heading: The Institute in Exile
sections.body:
In 1923 the Institute for Social Research was founded in Frankfurt, funded by Felix Weil, the son of a wealthy grain merchant. It aimed to study society through Marxism (Day 63) without being tied to any political party. When Max Horkheimer (1895–1973) became director in 1930, he turned it toward an ambitious interdisciplinary project combining philosophy, sociology, economics and psychoanalysis. Its circle is now called the **Frankfurt School**.

Its members were mostly Jewish and left-wing, and in 1933 the Nazis closed the Institute. It moved via Geneva to New York, where it was affiliated with Columbia University. Key figures included Theodor W. Adorno (1903–1969), philosopher, sociologist and trained musician; Herbert Marcuse (1898–1979), a former student of Heidegger (Day 76); the psychoanalyst Erich Fromm; and, more loosely, the brilliant essayist Walter Benjamin (1892–1940). Benjamin fled France in 1940 but, fearing he would be handed to the Gestapo at the Spanish border town of Portbou, took his own life.

In 1937 Horkheimer published an essay defining the group's approach, “Traditional and Critical Theory”. **Traditional theory**, modelled on natural science, describes and explains the world as it is, treating its own position as neutral. **Critical theory** asks how society came to be this way, whose interests its structures serve, and how they might be changed. Its aim is not just to understand society but to emancipate people from domination. And it is reflective: it asks how social conditions shape knowledge itself, including the theorist's own.

Why had Marx's prediction of revolution in advanced countries failed? Why did workers vote for fascists? These questions led the Frankfurt School beyond economics to culture, psychology and the family, the places where people learn to accept their own domination.

sections.heading: Dialectic of Enlightenment and the Culture Industry
sections.body:
During the war, Horkheimer and Adorno, by then in California, wrote *Dialectic of Enlightenment* (circulated in 1944, published in 1947). Its thesis is dark: enlightenment itself has a self-destructive tendency. The Enlightenment (Days 54–57) promised to free humanity from myth and fear through reason. But the reason that triumphed was **instrumental reason**: thinking about the most efficient means to given ends, without asking whether the ends are good. Reason that masters nature turns into reason that manages people, measures everything, and can organise a death camp as efficiently as a factory. In their words, enlightenment reverts to mythology. The book's title borrows Hegel's term (Day 59): enlightenment produces its own opposite.

The book's most famous chapter attacks the **culture industry**, a phrase they chose instead of “mass culture” to stress that it is not culture arising from the masses, but culture manufactured for them, like cars. Living in Los Angeles near Hollywood, they analysed films, radio, popular music and magazines as products of industrial capitalism. Their claims:

- **Standardisation.** Hit songs, films and stories follow formulas with interchangeable parts; you know how a film will end from its first minutes.
- **Pseudo-individuality.** Small differences (a star's quirks, a product's colour) create an illusion of choice and personality in identical goods.
- **Passivity and conformity.** Entertainment trains people to accept the world as it is. Amusement is a prolongation of work: it refreshes workers so they can return to the same routines, and it leaves no room for reflection.
- **Domination through pleasure.** Unlike the open terror of fascism, the culture industry rules by giving people what they think they want.

Adorno was notoriously scornful of jazz, which he heard as standardised commercial music. Many critics think this shows the limits of his elitism and his ear: he missed jazz's creativity and its roots in Black American experience. His famous remark of 1949, that to write poetry after Auschwitz is barbaric, expressed his conviction that culture could not carry on as if nothing had happened; he later qualified it.

Walter Benjamin offered a more hopeful view. In his essay on the work of art in the age of mechanical reproduction (1935–36), he argued that photography and film destroy the **aura** of a unique original artwork, its quasi-religious authority. This could be dangerous, as in fascist spectacle, but also democratic: art becomes available to everyone and open to political use.

sections.heading: Marcuse, Habermas and the Public Sphere
sections.body:
Herbert Marcuse stayed in the United States and became an unexpected celebrity. His *One-Dimensional Man* (1964) argued that advanced industrial society creates **false needs**, desires for consumer goods that keep people working and buying, and absorbs every opposition, so that even protest becomes a product. People lose the second dimension of thought, the ability to imagine something radically different from what exists. The book inspired the student movements of the 1960s, a role Adorno, who returned to Frankfurt in 1949, viewed with deep unease.

The most influential member of the second generation is Jürgen Habermas (born 1929). He agreed with much of the critique of instrumental reason but thought Adorno and Horkheimer had become too pessimistic; they had left no foundation for criticism itself. Habermas looked for a better form of reason.

In *The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere* (1962), he traced the rise of the **public sphere** in eighteenth-century Europe: coffeehouses in London, salons in Paris, reading societies in Germany, newspapers and journals. In these spaces private individuals came together to discuss public matters, in principle treating each other as equals and judging arguments on their merits rather than on the speaker's rank. Public opinion formed this way could hold state power to account.

The ideal was never fully real. Habermas acknowledged that this public was mostly educated, property-owning men, and later critics such as Nancy Fraser stressed the exclusion of women, workers and minorities, who formed their own counter-publics. But he argued that the ideal was valuable and had decayed. In the twentieth century, mass media owned by large corporations, advertising, public relations and party machines turned citizens from active participants into a passive audience to be managed. Public debate became staged display, a kind of **refeudalisation** in which the powerful perform before the public rather than reasoning with it.

Later, in *The Theory of Communicative Action* (1981), Habermas developed the idea of **communicative reason**: when we argue sincerely, we implicitly aim at agreement reached only through the force of the better argument, free from coercion. That ideal, he believed, gives critical theory a standard by which to judge distorted communication.

sections.heading: Hannah Arendt: The Origins of Totalitarianism
sections.body:
Hannah Arendt (1906–1975) was never part of the Frankfurt School, and she disliked several of its members, but she shared their experience of exile and their central question. Born near Hanover and raised in Königsberg, Kant's city (Day 55), she went to Marburg in 1924 to study with Heidegger and, still a teenager, began a secret love affair with him. She then wrote her doctoral dissertation on the concept of love in Augustine (Day 30) under Karl Jaspers. In 1933 she was briefly arrested by the Gestapo for researching Nazi antisemitism, then fled to Paris. In 1940 she was interned in the Gurs camp in southern France, escaped, and in 1941 reached New York. She was stateless until she became an American citizen in 1951.

That year she published *The Origins of Totalitarianism*. Arendt argued that **totalitarianism**, as seen in Nazi Germany and Stalin's Soviet Union, was a genuinely new form of government, not just an extreme tyranny. Ordinary tyrants want obedience; totalitarian movements want total domination, the reshaping of human nature itself. Its features include:

- **Ideology**: a single idea, the laws of Nature (race) or History (class), from which everything is deduced with iron logic, immune to facts.
- **Terror**: not just to punish opponents but to make the ideology come true, eliminating whole categories of people declared doomed by history or nature.
- **Atomised masses**: totalitarianism thrives among lonely, uprooted people cut off from class, community and shared public life. Loneliness, she argued, is its common ground.
- **The camps**: laboratories in which the belief that everything is possible was tested, destroying first the legal person, then the moral person, then individuality itself.

Her own statelessness gave her a sharp insight into human rights. The refugees of the 1930s, she observed, had lost the protection of any government, and supposedly inalienable rights of man proved worthless the moment they were no longer citizens of anywhere. What they had lost was the **right to have rights**: membership in a political community willing to guarantee them.

In *The Human Condition* (1958) she distinguished labour, work and action, and praised political **action**, people appearing before one another in public, speaking and acting together, as the highest human activity. Its condition is **plurality**, the fact that we are many and different, and its hope is **natality**: every birth brings the capacity to begin something new.

sections.heading: Eichmann in Jerusalem and the Banality of Evil
sections.body:
In 1960 Israeli agents captured Adolf Eichmann in Argentina and brought him to Jerusalem for trial. Arendt covered the trial for *The New Yorker*, and in 1963 published *Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil*.

What struck her was the gap between the enormity of the deeds and the shallowness of the man. Eichmann did not seem to be driven by fanatical hatred or demonic cruelty. He was a careerist who wanted promotion, obeyed orders, took pride in his logistical efficiency and spoke in official jargon and stock phrases. He even claimed, surprisingly, to have lived according to Kant's moral precepts, distorting the categorical imperative (Day 56) into obedience to the Führer's will. What he displayed, Arendt concluded, was not stupidity but **thoughtlessness**: an inability to think from the standpoint of anyone else.

The **banality of evil** does not mean that the Holocaust was banal or that Eichmann was innocent. Arendt supported his execution. It means that monstrous evil can be done by people who are not monsters, through careerism, conformity and the failure to think. That made the problem more frightening, not less: such people are everywhere.

The book caused a storm. Arendt's brief, sharp criticism of the Jewish Councils, community leaders forced by the Nazis to help organise deportations, struck many readers as cruel and unfair to victims in impossible situations. Her friend Gershom Scholem wrote that she lacked love of the Jewish people; she replied that she had never loved any people, only her friends. Her ironic tone also offended many.

Historians have challenged her portrait too. Bettina Stangneth's *Eichmann Before Jerusalem* (2011), drawing on interviews Eichmann gave to Nazi sympathisers in Argentina in the 1950s, shows him boasting of his work as a convinced antisemite who regretted not killing more Jews. On this evidence, the dull bureaucrat in the glass booth was partly a performance to save his life. Yet many scholars think the concept survives even if Eichmann was a poor example: Stanley Milgram's obedience experiments from 1961 onward, and historian Christopher Browning's *Ordinary Men* (1992), on a police battalion of middle-aged reservists who shot thousands of Jews, suggest that ordinary people can indeed be drawn into atrocity.

In her last, unfinished work, *The Life of the Mind*, Arendt asked whether the activity of thinking itself, the habit of stopping to examine what we are doing, as Socrates did (Day 9), might help protect us from doing evil.

modernConnection.title: The Feed, the Public Sphere and Thoughtless Systems
modernConnection.body:
Each of today's thinkers looks newly relevant in the age of platforms.

Adorno and Horkheimer described a culture industry that standardised products while flattering each consumer's sense of individuality. Today, streaming services and social platforms use recommendation algorithms that study what millions of people watch and click, then serve each of us a personalised stream. Formats spread rapidly, songs are sometimes shaped to grab attention within seconds, and sequels and reboots dominate cinema. Pseudo-individuality has become a business model: *for you*, the feed says, about content optimised for everyone.

Habermas's public sphere offers a way to judge social media. The internet once seemed to promise a global coffeehouse where anyone could join debate as equals. In practice, public discussion often runs on platforms owned by a few companies and optimised for engagement, which can reward outrage, spectacle and tribal loyalty rather than the force of the better argument. Habermas himself returned to the topic in 2022 with a short book on a new structural transformation of the public sphere, worrying that digital media fragment the public into bubbles.

Arendt's banality of evil speaks to how harm happens in large organisations: the employee who processes a cruel policy because it is the procedure, or the engineer who optimises a system without asking what it does to people. When harm is spread across many hands, each can feel like a mere functionary.

But be careful with these parallels. The Frankfurt critique can become condescending, as if audiences were simply passive dupes; research on fan communities and online creativity shows people remixing, criticising and resisting culture. Social media has also given voice to people historically excluded from the old public sphere. And comparing an office bureaucrat to Eichmann trivialises genocide. The honest use of these thinkers is as warning lights: ask who designs your choices, whether your public debates are reasoning or performance, and whether you are thinking about what your work actually does.

vocabulary.definition: The Frankfurt School's approach to social theory, which aims not only to describe society but to expose the structures of domination within it and help emancipate people.
vocabulary.example: A critical theory of advertising would ask not just how ads work but whose interests they serve and what desires they create.

vocabulary.definition: Reasoning concerned only with the most efficient means to given ends, without asking whether the ends themselves are good.
vocabulary.example: Designing the fastest railway timetable for deportations is a chilling case of instrumental reason.

vocabulary.definition: Adorno and Horkheimer's term for the mass production of standardised cultural goods, such as films and pop music, which they argued promote passivity and conformity.
vocabulary.example: A film studio producing a tenth formula sequel because it is a safe investment illustrates the culture industry.

vocabulary.definition: Habermas's term for the arena in which private individuals come together to discuss matters of common concern as equals, forming public opinion that can hold power to account.
vocabulary.example: Eighteenth-century coffeehouses where readers debated newspaper articles were early sites of the public sphere.

vocabulary.definition: For Arendt, a new form of government that seeks total domination through ideology and terror, aiming to reshape reality and human nature, as in Nazi Germany and Stalin's Soviet Union.
vocabulary.example: Arendt argued that totalitarianism differs from ordinary tyranny because it seeks to control not just actions but thought itself.

vocabulary.definition: Arendt's phrase for the idea that great evil can be committed by ordinary, unthinking people motivated by careerism and conformity rather than by demonic hatred.
vocabulary.example: A clerk who signs deportation orders without reflection, thinking only of his promotion, illustrates the banality of evil.

vocabulary.definition: Arendt's phrase for membership in a political community that will recognise and protect a person's rights, without which abstract human rights prove empty.
vocabulary.example: A stateless refugee with no country to protect her has lost what Arendt called the right to have rights.

vocabulary.definition: Arendt's term for the human capacity to begin something new, grounded in the fact of birth, which makes political action and freedom possible.
vocabulary.example: A small protest that grows into a movement no one predicted reflects Arendt's natality.

thinkingExercise.title: Audit Your Culture and Your Thinking
thinkingExercise.prompt: Use the Frankfurt School and Arendt to examine your own media diet and your place in large systems.
steps: List the last five films, shows, songs or videos you consumed. How did you find them: your own search, a friend, or an algorithm? How similar are they to each other?
Choose one and analyse it like Adorno: what formula does it follow, and what does it encourage you to accept or feel about the world?
Now defend it against Adorno: what in it is creative, surprising or critical? Is his critique fair?
Think of an organisation you belong to (school, workplace, club). Is there any routine you follow that might cause harm you never think about? Describe it.
Write a paragraph answering Arendt's question: can the habit of thinking protect us from wrongdoing, or do people need something more?

summary: The Frankfurt School, founded in 1923 and driven into exile by the Nazis, developed critical theory: social analysis aimed at exposing domination and enabling emancipation.

In *Dialectic of Enlightenment*, Horkheimer and Adorno argued that instrumental reason turned enlightenment into new forms of domination, and that the culture industry produces standardised entertainment that encourages conformity.
Habermas traced the rise of a public sphere of rational debate and its decay under mass media and commercial pressures, and later grounded critique in communicative reason.
Hannah Arendt analysed totalitarianism as a new form of rule based on ideology, terror and atomised loneliness, and argued that stateless people lose the right to have rights.

Reporting on the Eichmann trial, Arendt coined the phrase banality of evil: great evil done through thoughtlessness rather than monstrous motives; later evidence about Eichmann complicates her portrait.

quiz.question: How does critical theory, as Horkheimer defined it, differ from traditional theory?
options: It rejects all empirical research
It focuses only on literature
It aims not only to describe society but to expose domination and help emancipate people
It is based entirely on natural science
quiz.explanation: Traditional theory describes the world as it is; critical theory asks whose interests social structures serve and how they might be changed.

quiz.question: What is instrumental reason?
options: Reasoning about the most efficient means to ends without questioning the ends themselves
Reasoning about musical instruments
The use of logic in mathematics
Reasoning based on religious faith
quiz.explanation: Horkheimer and Adorno argued that reason reduced to calculating means can serve any goal, including domination.

quiz.question: Adorno and Horkheimer chose the term culture industry to stress that popular culture arises spontaneously from the people.
quiz.explanation: They chose it precisely to reject that idea: the culture industry manufactures culture for the masses, like any industrial product.

quiz.question: A streaming service shows each user a personalised page of shows that all follow the same proven formulas. Which Frankfurt School idea fits best?
options: Natality
The right to have rights
Communicative reason
Pseudo-individuality in the culture industry
quiz.explanation: The personalised feel disguises standardised products, which is what Adorno and Horkheimer called pseudo-individuality.

quiz.question: According to Habermas, what happened to the public sphere in the twentieth century?
options: It finally included everyone as equals
Commercial mass media, advertising and public relations turned citizens into a passive audience
It moved entirely into universities
It was abolished by law
quiz.explanation: Habermas described a refeudalisation in which the powerful perform before the public rather than reasoning with it.

quiz.question: Which feature did Arendt think distinguished totalitarianism from ordinary tyranny?
options: It always arises from a military coup
It is only found in communist states
It seeks total domination through ideology and terror, aiming to reshape reality and human nature
It allows free elections but restricts the press
quiz.explanation: Tyranny wants obedience; totalitarianism wants total domination, using ideology and terror against whole categories of people.

quiz.question: By the banality of evil, Arendt meant that the Holocaust was a trivial event and Eichmann bore little responsibility.
quiz.explanation: She meant that great evil can be done by thoughtless, ordinary people; she held Eichmann fully responsible and supported his execution.

quiz.question: What does Bettina Stangneth's research on Eichmann suggest?
options: That Eichmann was innocent
That Eichmann was a committed antisemite whose dull bureaucrat persona in Jerusalem was partly a performance
That Arendt never attended the trial
That Eichmann was mentally ill
quiz.explanation: Interviews Eichmann gave in Argentina reveal him as an ideological antisemite, complicating Arendt's portrait of thoughtlessness.

quiz.question: Arendt argued that stateless refugees showed how abstract human rights can prove empty without membership in a political community.
quiz.explanation: This is her idea of the right to have rights, drawn partly from her own years as a stateless refugee.

quiz.question: Which is a common criticism of Adorno's view of popular culture?
options: It was too enthusiastic about Hollywood
It ignored capitalism
It relied on detailed audience surveys
It was elitist and treated audiences as passive dupes, as in his dismissal of jazz
quiz.explanation: Critics argue that Adorno underestimated audiences' creativity and missed the artistic and cultural depth of forms like jazz.

goDeeper.body:
Three advanced debates are worth exploring. The first is the **Habermas–Arendt contrast on politics**. Both prize public discussion, but differently. Habermas emphasises rational argument aimed at consensus; Arendt emphasises action and plurality, people appearing before others and beginning something new, with persuasion rather than proof. Arendt also drew a sharp line between the political and the social, arguing that modern politics had been swamped by economic questions of need and welfare. Critics, including many on the left, found this distinction untenable, since poverty and labour are surely political matters.

The second concerns **Arendt and Heidegger**. Her early love affair with Heidegger and her renewed friendship with him after the war, despite his Nazism (Day 76), troubled readers once it became widely known through Elżbieta Ettinger's 1995 book. Philosophically, many see Arendt's emphasis on plurality, natality and the shared world as a deliberate answer to Heidegger's solitary authenticity and being-toward-death. Where he stressed mortality, she stressed birth.

The third is the **later history of critical theory**. Axel Honneth, Habermas's successor in Frankfurt, developed a theory of recognition, arguing that social struggles are driven by experiences of disrespect, which links critical theory back to Hegel. Nancy Fraser debated with him whether justice is mainly about recognition or redistribution. Critical theory in this broad sense later influenced feminist, postcolonial and critical race theory, so that today the phrase can refer to a large family of approaches, sometimes fiercely contested in public debate. Distinguishing the original Frankfurt School from these later developments is a useful scholarly habit.

readings.note: Read chapters 1–3 and the Postscript, where she answers her critics.

readings.title: Dialectic of Enlightenment
readings.author: Max Horkheimer and Theodor W. Adorno
readings.note: The chapter “The Culture Industry: Enlightenment as Mass Deception” is the most accessible part.

readings.title: The Origins of Totalitarianism
readings.author: Hannah Arendt
readings.note: Long; start with the final chapter, “Ideology and Terror”, and the chapter on the decline of the nation-state and the rights of man.

readings.author: Stuart Jeffries
readings.note: A lively, readable group biography of the Frankfurt School.

questions: Is the culture industry critique still convincing in an age when anyone can make and publish content?
Does the banality of evil remain a useful idea even if Eichmann himself was a fanatic?
What would a healthy public sphere look like online? Who should be responsible for building it?
